plat-product-mindset-for-platforms.core: A product mindset makes platforms developers actually want: reject the Field of Dreams, define value as reduced cognitive load, research users, share outcome roadmaps, start with a Thinnest Viable Platform, cross the adoption chasm, market internally and measure adoption, satisfaction and outcomes.

first_principles.problem: Platforms built on assumptions and shipped without product practices go unused.

analogy.title: Running an internal startup
analogy.story: Customers (developers), product-market fit, an MVP, launches, marketing and metrics.
analogy.breaks: Some capabilities must be mandated, but they still deserve good UX.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A platform the organisation relies on and values.

check.q: What's the core shift in a platform 'product mindset'?
check.a: Treating developers as customers whose needs and adoption define the platform's value.

plat-internal-developer-platforms-backst.core: An Internal Developer Platform tames tool sprawl: a solid platform engine with APIs underneath, and a portal such as Backstage on top, providing a software catalogue (ownership and dependencies), scaffolding templates (golden-path starts), plugins and self-service actions (no tickets) and TechDocs (docs as code).

first_principles.problem: Scattered tools, unknown ownership, slow setup and ticket queues waste developer time.
truths: Metadata and docs near code stay fresh.

analogy.title: An airport's operations hub
analogy.story: A central board (catalogue), standard check-in kits (templates), self-service kiosks (actions) and posted instructions (docs), backed by real operations behind the scenes.
analogy.breaks: Backstage needs ongoing investment (plugins, upgrades), so staff it like a product.

example.title: A developer's day with an IDP
example.outcome: a developer cockpit backed by a real platform.

check.a: The software catalogue, software templates (scaffolder), plugins and self-service actions, and TechDocs.

plat-cognitive-load-team-topologies.core: Managing cognitive load with Team Topologies: the infrastructure stack overflows developers, so use Conway's Law deliberately, organise into four team types (mostly stream-aligned, supported by platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams), choose interaction modes explicitly, start with a TVP and measure load.

first_principles.problem: Developers expected to master everything deliver slowly and burn out.
truths: Team design shapes systems and load.

analogy.title: A hospital organised for patient flow
analogy.story: Ward teams focus on patients while labs, specialists and trainers support them through clear protocols.
analogy.breaks: Topologies evolve, so revisit them as products and teams change.

example.title: Restructuring an engineering org
flow: Load scores and lead time improve
example.outcome: an organisation designed around human limits.

check.q: Why does Team Topologies focus on cognitive load?
check.a: Team capacity to understand and own systems is limited, and overloaded teams slow down and make more mistakes.

plat-abstraction-design-leaky-golden-pat.core: Abstraction design simplifies complexity responsibly: hide what doesn't matter, accept that abstractions leak and design for it (escape hatches, progressive disclosure), pave golden paths instead of mandating, use automated guardrails instead of gates, express intent over implementation and cut the cognitive load tax.

first_principles.problem: Raw infrastructure overwhelms developers, while poor abstractions frustrate them and hide failures.

analogy.title: Designing a modern car
analogy.story: A simple dashboard, warning lights that explain problems, a sport mode for experts, lane-keeping assist instead of road closures and 'destination' satnav instead of turn-by-turn engine control.
analogy.breaks: Every abstraction is a product that needs maintenance and iteration.

example.title: A platform service spec rollout

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Faster, safer delivery with fewer tickets.

example.outcome: abstractions that accelerate rather than constrain.

check.q: What's the difference between a golden path and a guardrail?
check.a: A golden path guides teams to the recommended way, while guardrails automatically enforce safety boundaries on whatever path they take.

plat-metrics-dora-space-adoption.core: Measuring platform success combines DORA (throughput and stability of delivery), SPACE (multi-dimensional developer experience, including wellbeing) and adoption metrics (coverage, activation, engagement, satisfaction), linked into a causal story from platform use to better experience to faster, safer delivery.

first_principles.problem: Without the right metrics, platform value is invisible and priorities are guesses.

analogy.title: A complete business dashboard
analogy.story: Customer usage, customer happiness and revenue results, each meaningful only alongside the others.
analogy.breaks: Metrics are for learning. Using them to rank individuals destroys trust.

check.q: Why should platform teams never measure productivity with activity metrics alone?
check.a: Activity (commits, lines of code) is easily gamed and doesn't reflect outcomes or developer wellbeing.

plat-multi-cloud-strategy-lock-in-abstra.core: Multi-cloud balances freedom and complexity: be clear why you want it, analyse lock-in as switching cost versus value, abstract selectively (avoiding lowest-common-denominator traps), respect data gravity in exit plans, distrust cost arbitrage, and use proven patterns like best-of-breed and segmentation with a common control plane.

first_principles.problem: Dogmatic multi-cloud multiplies cost and complexity without the expected benefits.

analogy.title: Diversifying investments wisely
analogy.story: Spread where it reduces real risk, but don't pay so many fees managing accounts that it erases the returns.
analogy.breaks: For most organisations, multi-region on one cloud gives better resilience per dollar.

check.q: What's usually a more cost-effective resilience strategy than multi-cloud?
check.a: Multi-region (or multi-AZ) architecture within a single cloud provider.

plat-platform-economics-roi-build-vs-buy.core: Platform economics justifies and steers investment: calculate ROI from the efficiency dividend, add the indirect value of stability, onboarding and risk reduction, decide build vs buy on full TCO (remembering the iceberg), and allocate costs through showback or chargeback with simple, incentive-aligned pricing.

first_principles.problem: Platform teams that can't explain their value or costs lose funding and make poor build decisions.

analogy.title: Running an internal utility company
analogy.story: Show the value delivered, decide which plants to build or contract, account for maintenance, and bill customers fairly and simply.
analogy.breaks: Financial metrics can't capture all strategic value, so pair them with a narrative.

example.title: An annual platform business review
flow: Build vs buy: replaced homegrown CI with SaaS (−1.5 FTE)
example.outcome: a platform run as a sound business.

check.q: What are the three main levers in platform economics covered here?
check.a: Demonstrating ROI and value, making build-vs-buy decisions on full TCO, and allocating costs through showback or chargeback.

plat-deprecation-engineering-scream-test.core: Deprecation engineering removes zombie infrastructure deliberately: inventory usage, use scream tests only as a careful last resort, prefer escalating brownouts, automate migrations with codemods that open PRs, and manage psychological resistance with clear reasons, support and firm deadlines.

first_principles.problem: Never deleting anything creates costly, insecure, confusing tool sprawl.

analogy.title: Retiring an old bridge
analogy.story: Survey who uses it, announce the closure, reduce lanes gradually, build and guide traffic to the new bridge, and close the old one on schedule.
analogy.breaks: Critical legacy systems may need a longer, staged replacement.

example.title: Deprecating API v1

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: v1 removed with no major incident.

example.outcome: a platform that can shed its past.

check.q: Why are brownouts safer than scream tests?
check.a: They give gradual, scheduled and clearly communicated signals rather than an abrupt shutdown that surprises users.

plat-tech-radar-strategy-adopt-hold.core: A tech radar fights résumé-driven sprawl by communicating risk in four rings (Adopt, Trial, Assess, Hold) across quadrants, governed collaboratively with evidence-based proposals, and paired with a high bar against language proliferation.

first_principles.problem: Unguided technology choices fragment the stack, multiply support costs and orphan services.
truths: Every technology has a support cost.

analogy.title: A trusted restaurant guide
analogy.story: Recommended, worth a try, one to watch, avoid, curated by experienced diners with evidence.
analogy.breaks: The radar must enable innovation, not block it, so keep the Trial path real.

example.title: A quarterly radar update
flow: New language request → declined; Trial for Rust only in data plane
example.outcome: technology governance that's transparent and fair.

check.q: What's the purpose of a tech radar?
check.a: To communicate transparently which technologies are recommended, on trial, being assessed or on hold, guiding consistent choices.

plat-adoption-psychology-shadow-it.core: Adoption psychology explains why good tools fail: habit and switching costs. Cross the chasm from visionaries to pragmatists with a beachhead and a whole product, and treat shadow IT as a signal of unmet needs, absorbing it by paving an easier sanctioned path.

first_principles.problem: Platforms stall at early adoption and fight endless shadow IT.

analogy.title: Urban planning with desire paths
analogy.story: Pave where people already walk, build a complete route for the first neighbourhood, then extend it.
analogy.breaks: Some risks need enforcement, so combine paving with firm guardrails.

example.title: A platform adoption turnaround
example.outcome: platforms adopted because they're the best option.

check.q: How should platform teams respond to shadow IT?
check.a: Treat it as a signal of unmet needs and make the sanctioned path better and easier, rather than only banning it.

plat-governance-as-code-golden-path.core: Governance as code replaces PDFs with automation: vending-machine modules make compliance the default, drift detection catches ClickOps divergence, and preventive policy checks (OPA, Kyverno) block violations before they apply, all with clear feedback and exception paths.

first_principles.problem: Document-based governance is ignored, inconsistent and discovered too late.

analogy.title: Building safety in a modern city
analogy.story: Pre-certified building kits (modules), regular inspections (drift detection) and permit checks before construction (policy).
analogy.breaks: Automation can't judge everything, so keep a human review for exceptions.

check.q: Name the three layers of governance as code covered here.
check.a: Compliant vending-machine modules, drift detection and preventive policy checks.

plat-documentation-engineering-docs-as-c.core: Documentation engineering cures wiki rot by treating knowledge as a product: docs-as-code workflows (Markdown in Git, PR review, CI), diagrams-as-code, unified search with analytics, freshness metrics and ownership, managed with templates, tooling and success metrics.

first_principles.problem: Outdated, scattered and unfindable docs destroy trust and slow everyone down.

analogy.title: A well-run public library
analogy.story: Curated collections, a catalogue, librarians, renewal schedules and visitor feedback.
analogy.breaks: Culture matters: engineers have to value writing for any of this to work.

example.title: A docs platform roll-out
example.outcome: knowledge managed as a first-class product.

check.a: Managing documentation with developer workflows: plain-text files in Git, PR reviews, CI checks and automated publishing.

plat-technical-writing-docs-as-code-runb.core: Technical writing is the interface between humans and machines: apply clarity rules (audience, BLUF, specificity, examples), keep docs in sync through docs-as-code, write runbooks for stressed responders and choose the right document type (Diátaxis: tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation).

first_principles.problem: Unclear, drifting or mixed-purpose documentation causes errors, slow onboarding and prolonged incidents.

analogy.title: Designing signage for an airport
analogy.story: Clear wording, signs updated with every terminal change, emergency procedures posted, and different signs for arrivals, gates and information.
analogy.breaks: Writing quality needs feedback from real readers, so test with them.

check.q: What are the four Diátaxis documentation types?
check.a: Tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation.

plat-devrel-internal-evangelism.core: Internal DevRel prevents platforms failing silently: credible, hands-on evangelism and champions, high-touch office hours and hackathons, measurement through developer NPS and adoption funnels, and a feedback loop closed visibly with 'you said, we did'.

first_principles.problem: Good platform capabilities go unused because of low awareness, low trust and ignored feedback.

analogy.title: A beloved local bookshop
analogy.story: Knowledgeable staff recommend books, host events, ask what customers want and visibly stock it.
analogy.breaks: DevRel amplifies product quality and can't replace it.

example.title: A DevRel programme
example.outcome: a platform with an engaged developer community.

check.q: What's the most underrated DevRel skill according to this topic?
check.a: Visibly acting on feedback and communicating what changed, which is closing the loop.

plat-maturity-models-cncf-levels.core: Platform maturity models map the journey: Level 1 ad hoc (tribal knowledge, heroes), Level 2 managed (standards, but ticket queues), Level 3 optimised (self-service golden paths with guardrails, platform as product) and Level 4 strategic (the platform as business differentiator). Assess honestly and take the next step.

first_principles.problem: Organisations either stagnate in chaos or attempt leaps they can't support.
truths: Each level fixes the previous level's pain.

analogy.title: A city's development
analogy.story: From a frontier town, to a town with inspectors, to a city with self-service permits online, to a city whose infrastructure attracts global business.
analogy.breaks: Different dimensions mature at different speeds, so assess each one.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A steady climb with value at every step.

check.q: What's the defining characteristic of Level 3 platform maturity?
check.a: Self-service through golden paths and APIs with built-in guardrails, managed as a product.

plat-cnoe-reference-architecture.core: CNOE offers an opinionated-but-open blueprint for internal developer platforms, cutting through CNCF choice paralysis with a validated stack (Backstage, Argo CD, Crossplane, External Secrets, Kyverno), a focus on operational outcomes, and idpbuilder for running the reference locally.

first_principles.problem: Teams waste months choosing and integrating tools, producing fragile bespoke platforms.

analogy.title: A proven house plan
analogy.story: A plan used by many families, with options to swap fixtures, and a model home you can visit first.
analogy.breaks: Every organisation still needs integration work and ownership.

example.title: Bootstrapping an IDP with CNOE
flow: Adopt core stack, swap policy engine

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A platform in weeks, not quarters.

example.outcome: a de-risked path to a modern IDP.

plat-score-workload-specification.core: Score is a universal workload specification: developers describe containers, resources and service once in score.yaml, and platform-specific implementations (Compose, Kubernetes) translate it, injecting environment context so one spec runs everywhere, fitting above existing tools in a platform workflow.

first_principles.problem: Describing workloads differently per environment causes drift and 'works on my machine' failures.

analogy.title: Sheet music for software
analogy.story: One score, performed faithfully by any orchestra with the right musicians.
analogy.breaks: Adoption needs platform investment in implementations and provisioners.

example.title: A local-to-prod journey
flow: score-k8s in CI for staging and prod

plat-thick-vs-thin-wrappers-k8s.core: Kubernetes is a datacentre operating system, and platform teams choose how much to expose: thin wrappers (native API plus guardrails, flexible but demanding), thick wrappers (PaaS-like simplicity that leaks at the edges), or a layered mix chosen by workload diversity, skills, compliance and capacity.

first_principles.problem: One-size-fits-all wrappers either overwhelm developers or constrain experts.

analogy.title: Kitchen access in a restaurant group
analogy.story: Head chefs get the full professional kitchen; new cooks get a simplified station with recipes; both are in the same building.
analogy.breaks: Wrapper strategy needs revisiting as teams and workloads change.

example.title: A layered platform
flow: Escape lane: raw manifests with policies (thin)

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Simple for most people, powerful for experts.

example.outcome: the right abstraction for each audience.

check.a: Offering a thick, simple golden path for common workloads alongside thin, native access with guardrails for experts.
